title: Europe’s Ancient Landscapes May Have Been More Open Than We Thought
paragraphs: For many people, the original Europe is a vast, shady forest. A new study led by researchers at Aarhus University in Denmark challenges that image. Instead of relying on one kind of evidence, the team combined fossil pollen and plant remains, charcoal from ancient wildfires, chemical signatures in the teeth and bones of plant-eating animals, fossil insects and mammals, and environmental DNA preserved in sediments.

Their conclusion is that, for more than 20 million years, Europe was dominated by a shifting mosaic of trees, open spaces and flowering plants rather than continuous closed forest. The pattern appears under temperate conditions like today’s as well as in warmer and colder periods. The authors believe that large herbivores, including elephants, rhinoceroses, aurochs and bison, helped to maintain these open landscapes through grazing and ground disturbance.

The researchers draw a policy lesson from this. Senior author Jens-Christian Svenning says current reforestation practices are “on the wrong track”, pointing to schemes, such as Danish subsidies, that fund only dense forest planting. They recommend restoring mixed woodland-and-open habitats and large animals instead. It is worth remembering that this is a synthesis of past evidence, so some details remain uncertain, and other scientists may weigh the same records differently. The work appears in Biological Conservation.

questions.q: Why did the team use many types of evidence?
questions.a: No single type of evidence gives a complete picture.

questions.q: What do the authors say about reforestation schemes?
questions.a: They say some pay only for dense forest and are on the wrong track.
The study is a synthesis of past evidence, so some details are uncertain.
